extracted.intended_audience: researchers, conference organizers, journal editors, and policymakers interested in peer-review processes and bias
extracted.subtask_description: Empirical evaluation of reviewer bias comparing single-blind and double-blind peer review in a selective computer-science conference (WSDM 2017) using a controlled experiment where reviewers either have or lack access to author information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer anonymity model (single-blind vs double-blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether reviewers are aware of authors' names and affiliations (single-blind) or that information is hidden (double-blind).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines the two reviewing models compared in the study: 'single-blind,' in which reviewers are aware of the names and affiliations of paper authors, or 'double-blind,' in which this information is hidden. This is the central axis for assessing differences in reviewer behavior and decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled experiment design (four reviewers per paper)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper was reviewed by four committee members: two drawn from a pool with access to author information and two from a disjoint pool without such access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental setup detail used to isolate effects of author-identifying information. The information asymmetry persisted through bidding, reviewing, and entering scores, enabling direct comparison within the same set of papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer bidding behavior (number of bids)
rubrics_metrics.description: Measure of how many papers reviewers express interest in reviewing; single-blind reviewers typically bid for 22% fewer papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bidding behavior was analyzed (e.g., cumulative distribution function of number of bids for single- and double-blind reviewers). Differences in bidding indicate how anonymity affects which papers reviewers choose to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferential bidding for papers from top universities and companies
rubrics_metrics.description: Tendency of reviewers (in the single-blind condition) to preferentially bid for papers authored by researchers at top universities and companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed during the bidding stage: single-blind reviewers showed preference toward papers from top institutions/companies, implying affiliation-driven selection bias at the allocation stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation-for-acceptance bias by author fame and affiliation
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-blind reviewers were significantly more likely than double-blind reviewers to recommend acceptance for papers from famous authors, top universities, and top companies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantified by estimated odds multipliers: 1.63 for famous authors, 1.58 for top universities, and 2.10 for top companies. This metric captures how author identity/affiliation changes reviewers' acceptance recommendations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of odds multipliers / statistical modeling to quantify bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical estimation (odds multipliers) used to express how much more likely single-blind reviewers are to favor certain papers based on author attributes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper reports tangible odds multipliers (e.g., 1.63, 1.58, 2.10) as a principled way to quantify the magnitude of bias. Choice of such measures and models is a criterion for rigorous assessment of reviewer bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information asymmetry persistence across review stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the presence or absence of author information is maintained through bidding, review writing, and score entry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study deliberately preserves the information asymmetry through all stages (bidding, reviewing, entering scores) so that any observed differences can be attributed to access to author information rather than downstream processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual venue selectivity (acceptance rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characteristics of the evaluated venue, e.g., WSDM's selectivity (15.6% acceptance rate), used to contextualize the potential impact of bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venue selectivity matters when assessing the practical consequences of observed biases: in highly selective conferences, modest biases can materially affect which papers are accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise / committee composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of expert committee members who review full-length submissions; the composition of reviewer pools (disjoint pools for single- and double-blind) is part of the evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer expertise and how reviewer pools are drawn can influence outcomes; the study's use of expert committee members is a methodological criterion that affects generalizability of findings.
